topic_title: Thanksgiving Bulletin Boards for November: 9 Classroom Ideas
intro: A November board stays up for three or four weeks, so it needs to hold attention beyond the first day. The boards that work best give each student a piece to write on or decorate, which also covers a gratitude or writing lesson. Choose a backing that will carry into December, such as burlap or plain kraft paper, so you only swap the cutouts after Thanksgiving. Count your class before buying cutouts and add a few spares for new students and mistakes.

picks.description: A bare tree trunk made from twisted brown kraft paper, with each student writing one thing they are thankful for on a paper leaf, is the most adaptable November board. It fits any grade, since young children can write one word and older students a full sentence, and the tree fills up over the month as leaves are added. Pre-cut leaf cutouts in orange, red and yellow save hours of cutting, though tracing leaves from the playground is a nice science tie-in. Use a fade-resistant backing in pale blue or cream so the colors stand out. The trunk can stay up through winter with the leaves swapped for paper snowflakes in December. Staple the leaves loosely at one point so they look like they could blow away.
picks.best_for: Any grade wanting a gratitude writing board that grows all month
picks.skip_if: You need a finished board on day one with no student input
picks.quirky_fact: Crumpling and smoothing brown kraft paper a few times before stapling gives the tree trunk a bark-like texture.
picks.product_name: Fall Leaves Paper Cut-Outs Assorted Colors 48 Pack

picks.description: A large paper turkey body in the center with blank feathers fanned around it is a favorite in preschool and the early grades, because each child writes or draws on a feather and sees it become part of the bird. Make the body from brown paper with googly eyes and a red wattle, and give each student one feather in orange, red, yellow or brown. Kids who cannot yet write can dictate a word to an adult or draw a picture. The board takes about an hour to set up and fills in a single lesson. Unlike the leaf tree, it does not carry into December, so plan to replace it after the break. Smaller paper plate turkeys made by each student can line the border.
picks.best_for: Preschool to second grade classes doing a single gratitude lesson
picks.skip_if: You want one display that can stay up past Thanksgiving
picks.quirky_fact: Writing names on the back of each feather makes it easy to send them home in the right backpack after the board comes down.
picks.product_name: Turkey Bulletin Board Set with Feather Cut-Outs

picks.description: A row of paper pumpkins, one per student with a name written across it, makes a welcoming board that doubles as a class list for visitors. Green paper vines and curling ribbon tendrils connect the pumpkins across the board. Students can decorate their own pumpkin with a face, a fact about themselves or a fall word, which works well for early-grade writing practice. Because pumpkins are a general fall image, this board suits classes where Thanksgiving itself is not the focus. Mixed pumpkin sizes and shades of orange look more natural than identical cutouts. It is quick to make and easy to keep fresh: replace the pumpkins with paper mittens or snowmen in December and keep the student names.
picks.best_for: Classes that want a neutral fall board celebrating each student
picks.skip_if: You want a board focused on gratitude writing rather than names
picks.quirky_fact: Pumpkins are botanically fruits, which makes this board a natural lead-in to a lesson on seeds.
picks.product_name: Pumpkin Paper Cut-Outs 36 Pack for Bulletin Boards

picks.description: A giant paper pie divided into slices, one per student, works well for upper elementary and middle school because each slice holds a full sentence or short paragraph. Title it something like a slice of thanks or what our class is thankful for. Students write on a triangular slice of tan or orange paper, then the slices are assembled into a round pie with a brown crust edge. Larger classes can make two or three pies across the board. It pairs with a fractions lesson in younger grades, since the slices show halves, quarters and eighths. The pie is a recognizable Thanksgiving image without being tied to the historical story, so it suits most classrooms.
picks.best_for: Upper elementary and middle school students writing longer responses
picks.skip_if: Your students are not yet writing full sentences
picks.quirky_fact: Cutting the slices from one large paper circle first guarantees they fit back together into a full pie.
picks.product_name: Tagboard Paper Circles 12 inch Assorted Colors

picks.description: A border of overlapping paper leaves frames any November board and makes even plain backing paper look seasonal. Ready-made scalloped or die-cut leaf borders come in long rolls and staple on in minutes, while a handmade garland of student-cut leaves takes longer but involves the whole class. Choose a border in warm reds and oranges to sit against a neutral backing, and it can frame a gratitude tree, a pumpkin patch or a reading display. Many teachers keep a fall border up from late September through November, so one roll covers three months. Store it rolled loosely around a tube, not folded, so the edge stays flat for next year.
picks.best_for: Teachers who want one border that frames all of fall
picks.skip_if: Your board already has a busy patterned backing
picks.quirky_fact: Stapling borders at a slight angle into the corkboard holds them better than stapling straight in.
picks.product_name: Autumn Leaves Scalloped Bulletin Board Border 39 ft

picks.description: Burlap backing with a red plaid border gives a farmhouse-style board that looks good in hallways and front offices as well as classrooms. Burlap fabric rolls staple onto corkboard easily and hide old staple holes, and the texture means it never looks faded. Add a simple title in cutout letters, a few paper sunflowers or wheat stalks, and space for student work. The backing works through fall and into winter with only the accents swapped, which makes it one of the most reusable choices here. Burlap sheds fibers when cut, so cut it a few inches oversized and fold the edges under before stapling. It suits schools that want a seasonal look without a holiday theme.
picks.best_for: Hallway, office or library boards that need a long-lasting backing
picks.skip_if: You want a bright, student-made display for young children
picks.quirky_fact: Burlap is woven from jute fiber, the same plant fiber used in many natural area rugs.
picks.product_name: Burlap Fabric Roll 48 inch x 5 Yards Natural

picks.description: A paper horn of plenty spilling out fruits, vegetables and gourds is a classic Thanksgiving image and a good fit for a lesson on harvest and food. Students each make one item, such as an apple, ear of corn or pear, and write a thank-you or a fact about it before it is added to the spill. The cornucopia itself can be woven from strips of brown paper for texture. It takes more setup time than the leaf tree or pumpkin patch, but it gives a bold, colorful board that visitors notice from across a hallway. Older students can label each food with where it grows, which ties into geography or science units.
picks.best_for: Classes pairing the board with a harvest or nutrition lesson
picks.skip_if: You have little prep time before the board needs to go up
picks.quirky_fact: Cornucopia comes from the Latin words for horn and plenty.
picks.product_name: Construction Paper Assorted Colors 9 x 12 inch 500 Sheets

picks.description: Paper acorns, each with a student's goal for the rest of the term, turn a seasonal board into a classroom management tool. Title it along the lines of small acorns grow into mighty oaks, and have each student write one reading, math or behavior goal on an acorn cap. The board can stay up through winter as students move their acorn up a paper oak tree when they meet the goal. It works best from third grade up, where students can set and track a realistic goal. Because it is about growth rather than the holiday, it is a good choice for classes with mixed holiday traditions. Add a few oak leaves from the leaf cutout pack for color.
picks.best_for: Third grade and up, teachers wanting a board tied to goals
picks.skip_if: Your students are too young to set and track their own goals
picks.quirky_fact: Many oak trees take 20 years or more before they produce their first acorns.
picks.product_name: Acorn Paper Cut-Outs 36 Pack for Classroom

picks.description: A paper scarecrow holding a sign about fall books makes a reading display where each student adds a paper patch or crow with the title of a book they finished. Stuff the scarecrow's shirt with real straw or crumpled yellow tissue paper for texture. It suits libraries and reading corners and can track a class reading goal for November. The scarecrow is a fall image rather than a Thanksgiving one, so it can go up in October and stay through the month. It takes more crafting than other boards, so it works best for teachers who enjoy a hands-on project or have a parent volunteer. Keep the book entries short so the board stays readable from a few feet away.
picks.best_for: Reading corners and libraries tracking a November reading goal
picks.skip_if: You want a quick board you can put up in under an hour
picks.quirky_fact: Straw for the scarecrow is sold in small craft bags, so you do not need a full bale.

faqs.question: When should a Thanksgiving bulletin board go up?
faqs.answer: Most teachers put it up the first school week of November, right after Halloween decor comes down, so it stays up through the Thanksgiving break. If students are adding pieces, start the board with the title and backing on day one and let it fill over the following weeks, which keeps it interesting longer than a finished board.

faqs.question: How can I make a Thanksgiving board that is inclusive?
faqs.answer: Center the board on gratitude, harvest or autumn rather than on the historical story, since families mark the holiday differently and some students may not celebrate it. Prompts like what I am thankful for or something that helps me learn let every student take part. Leaves, pumpkins and acorns are neutral images that work for everyone.

faqs.question: What backing paper lasts best on a bulletin board?
faqs.answer: Fade-resistant paper or fabric holds color far longer than standard construction paper, which can fade within weeks near a sunny window. Burlap, felt or a plain flat bedsheet can also be stapled up and reused for months. A neutral backing lets you change borders and cutouts each season without stripping the whole board.

faqs.question: How do I change a Thanksgiving board for December?
faqs.answer: Keep the backing and border if they are neutral, then swap the cutouts. A gratitude tree can become a winter tree by replacing leaves with paper snowflakes, and a burlap harvest board works with paper mittens or pine branches. Save student pieces in a folder so families can take them home after the break.

faqs.question: What age groups suit these boards?
faqs.answer: Turkey feathers, pumpkin name patches and leaf trees suit preschool to second grade, where students write a word or a short sentence. Older students do better with the pie board, goal-setting acorns or reading boards, where each piece holds a longer sentence or a book title. Any of them can be adapted by changing how much writing each piece asks for.

answer: A gratitude leaf tree, a thankful turkey with student-written feathers, and a pumpkin patch with a name on each pumpkin are the strongest November boards. All three let every student add something, and that is the deciding factor: a board kids fill themselves gets read, while a purely decorative one gets ignored.
method: Picked from Pinterest's trending searches for Thanksgiving bulletin boards in November, then ordered by how much each board involves students, how long it takes to put up, and how much of it can be reused in later seasons.
